title: Shared-link upload runs as the link owner, so the livePhotoVideoId owner check can never fail
summary:
# Shared-link upload runs as the link owner, so the livePhotoVideoId owner check can never fail

## Summary

An anonymous visitor holding an upload-enabled share link can hide any video belonging to the link owner,
and then read that video's metadata and stream it in full through the same anonymous key, including videos
that were never shared and on links where downloads are disabled.

The guard that should stop this exists and is bypassed rather than absent. For a share-key request the
authenticated principal *is* the link owner, so the comparison it makes can never be true.

Confirmed on the released `v3.1.0` image, `sourceCommit 8aa95c67`. Byte-identical on main at `a9a99cff`.

## Mechanism

`server/src/services/auth.service.ts` resolves a share key to the owner:

```ts
async validateSharedLinkKey(key: string | string[]): Promise<AuthDto> {
  ...
  return { user: sharedLink.user, sharedLink };
}
```

So `auth.user.id === sharedLink.userId` for an anonymous caller. Every downstream
`something.ownerId !== auth.user.id` guard silently evaluates to false.

`POST /assets` accepts share keys, at `asset-media.controller.ts:52`:

```ts
@Authenticated({ permission: Permission.AssetUpload, sharedLink: true })
```

and passes `auth.user.id` into `onBeforeLink` in `server/src/utils/asset.util.ts:145`:

```ts
if (motionAsset.ownerId !== userId) {
  throw new BadRequestException('Live photo video does not belong to the user');
}

if (motionAsset && motionAsset.visibility === AssetVisibility.Timeline) {
  await assetRepository.update({ id: livePhotoVideoId, visibility: AssetVisibility.Hidden });
  await eventRepository.emit('AssetHide', { assetId: motionAsset.id, userId });
}
```

The error string shows the restriction was intended. `livePhotoVideoId` is a plain field on the upload form,
so the caller picks the target.

## Proof

Same target asset, same request, only the principal differs. This is the whole finding in two lines.

```
logged-in outsider  -> 400 "Live photo video does not belong to the user"
anonymous share key -> 201, owner's video flipped to Hidden
```

After the anonymous request, on the same key with no Authorization header:

```
GET /assets/VID           400 before  ->  200 after, full metadata
GET /assets/VID/video/playback  404 before  ->  200 after, bytes identical to the owner's file
```

The owner's timeline loses the asset. A second video left untouched stays visible throughout, so this is
targeted and not a side effect of the upload.

Negative controls:

- `allowUpload=false` on the link: 401, target unchanged.
- No key at all: 401.
- A real logged-in outsider account against the same targets: 400, as quoted above. That is what proves the
  vacuous comparison rather than assuming it.

## Relationship to GHSA-hvq7-hq9r-8gjr

That advisory is properly fixed and I want to say so plainly. Commit `6ba17bb86` deleted the
`Permission.AssetShare` case from `checkSharedLinkAccess` outright, so a share key now falls through to
`default: return new Set<string>()` and gets no `AssetShare` access at all. The same commit removed
`sharedLink: true` from `PUT /shared-links/:id/assets` and the album asset-add routes.

`POST /assets` kept `sharedLink: true`, and it reaches a pre-existing owner asset by UUID through
`livePhotoVideoId`. So this is not a regression of that fix and not the same sink. It is the same
principal-level root cause on a route the route-by-route hardening did not visit.
